questions.stem: In the mid-nineteenth century, Moritz Lazarus and Heymann Steinthal founded a journal for Volkerpsychologie. This approach aimed to study:
options: the shared mental life of peoples, such as their language, myths and customs
single neurons in the brain using electrical recordings and powerful microscopes
the unconscious conflicts of individual patients through dream analysis
learning in animals placed in mazes and puzzle boxes in a laboratory
questions.explanation: Volkerpsychologie (often translated as 'folk' or 'peoples' psychology') studied the collective mind of a people through products such as language, myth and custom. It is an early example of treating the group, not just the individual, as a subject for psychology.

questions.stem: In the Stanford Prison Experiment (1971), male university students were randomly assigned to be guards or prisoners in a mock prison. Why was it stopped after six days instead of the planned two weeks?
options: Guards became increasingly abusive and prisoners showed severe distress
Prisoners took control of the prison and locked the guards in their cells
Funding ran out because the study was much more expensive than expected
Participants were bored and asked to leave because nothing was happening
questions.explanation: Some guards became harsh and humiliating and several prisoners showed signs of acute distress, so the study was ended early. Zimbardo concluded that the situation and roles, rather than personality, drove the behaviour.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest criticism of Zimbardo's conclusion that the prison roles alone caused the guards' behaviour?
options: Guards may have acted as they believed the researchers wanted, and Zimbardo ran the prison himself
Participants were randomly assigned to roles, so personality differences fully explain the results
The study lasted too long, so the guards became tired and stopped following the rules
The prisoners were all paid actors who had been told exactly how to behave beforehand
questions.explanation: Demand characteristics and Zimbardo's dual role as researcher and 'superintendent' mean guards may have followed what they thought was expected; later analyses suggest guards were encouraged to be tough. Random assignment was a strength, not a weakness.

questions.stem: In the BBC Prison Study (2002), Reicher and Haslam set up a mock prison without telling the guards how to behave. What happened?
options: The guards quickly became cruel and abusive, exactly as they had in the Stanford study
Both groups refused to take part and the study was abandoned on the first day
The prisoners accepted the guards' authority without question for the whole study
The guards did not form a shared identity, while the prisoners did and challenged them
questions.explanation: The guards were reluctant to use their power and never became a cohesive group, while the prisoners developed a shared identity and challenged the guards, and the regime broke down. Reicher and Haslam explained this with social identity theory.

questions.stem: How does the BBC Prison Study challenge the explanation drawn from the Stanford Prison Experiment?
options: It suggests people do not adopt roles automatically but act on shared group identity
It shows that people always become cruel when given power, whatever the situation
It proves that personality is the only cause of behaviour in a prison setting
It shows that mock prisons cannot be studied, because no one behaves differently in them
questions.explanation: Reicher and Haslam argued that tyranny is not a natural response to a role; people act collectively when they share a social identity, and leadership shapes what that identity means. This contrasts with Zimbardo's claim that roles alone produce abuse.

questions.stem: When Milgram moved his obedience study from Yale University to a run-down office in Bridgeport, obedience fell from 65% to about 48%. Which factor does this show?
options: The distance between teacher and learner affects obedience
The number of confederates present affects conformity
The personality of the participant fully explains obedience
The perceived legitimacy of the setting affects obedience
questions.explanation: Obedience fell, though not dramatically, when the prestige of the institution was removed, suggesting a legitimate setting increases obedience. Proximity to the learner was a different variation.

questions.stem: In one of Milgram's variations, the participant was one of three 'teachers', and the other two (confederates) refused to continue. Full obedience dropped to about 10%. This suggests that:
options: the learner's cries had no influence on any of the participants
participants obeyed because the shocks were known to be fake
seeing others disobey makes it easier for a person to resist authority
people obey much more when they are part of a larger group of teachers
questions.explanation: Rebellious peers gave participants social support and a model for refusing, sharply reducing obedience. This links to Asch's finding that one dissenter reduces conformity.

questions.stem: Diana Baumrind (1964) criticised Milgram's study on ethical grounds. Which concern was central?
options: Participants were told the true aim, so the study could never measure real obedience at all
Too few participants were used, so the findings had no statistical value
The learner was really harmed by electric shocks during the experiment
Participants were deceived and put under severe stress without proper protection from harm
questions.explanation: Baumrind argued that the deception and intense stress were not justified and could harm participants' self-image and trust in authority. The learner was a confederate and received no real shocks.

questions.stem: In Asch's line-judgement studies, when participants wrote their answers privately instead of saying them aloud, conformity dropped sharply. This suggests the conformity was mainly:
options: normative, driven by the wish to fit in and avoid rejection
informational, driven by real uncertainty about the right answer
obedience, driven by direct orders from an authority figure
social loafing, driven by reduced effort when in a group
questions.explanation: If people conform only when others can hear them, they are complying publicly to avoid disapproval while privately disagreeing; this is normative social influence. Informational influence would change private judgements too.

questions.stem: Asch's studies used male American college students in the early 1950s. Which criticism concerns this context?
options: The line task was so hard that every participant was truly unsure of the correct answer
Participants knew all the others were confederates, so the results are invalid
Conformity cannot be measured in a laboratory, so the results tell us nothing
Conformity levels may reflect the culture of that era and group, limiting generalisation
questions.explanation: The 1950s United States has been described as a conformist period, and later replications in other times and cultures found varied rates, so the findings may be partly a product of their context. The line task was in fact easy when people judged alone.

questions.stem: In 1964 Kitty Genovese was murdered in New York, and a newspaper reported that 38 witnesses did nothing. What did later investigations find?
options: Hundreds of people saw the attack, which made the bystander effect even larger
Far fewer people saw the attack clearly, and some did call police or try to help
Exactly 38 people watched the whole attack and none of them made any response at all
There were no witnesses at all, and the case had nothing to do with bystanders
questions.explanation: Later reviews found that few people saw the attack clearly, several heard only parts of it, and some called police or went to help. The case inspired valuable research, but it is an example of how a media story can become an inaccurate 'classic'.

questions.stem: In Latane and Darley's (1968) smoke-filled room study, participants alone usually reported the smoke, but few did when sitting with two confederates who ignored it. This is best explained by:
options: pluralistic ignorance, using others' calm to interpret the situation
diffusion of responsibility, because the smoke was someone else's fault
social facilitation, because others improved performance on easy tasks
deindividuation, because participants felt anonymous in the room
questions.explanation: When others appear unconcerned, people conclude the situation is not an emergency; this is pluralistic ignorance at the 'interpret' step. Diffusion of responsibility, where each person assumes someone else will act, was shown in the seizure study.

questions.stem: In Darley and Latane's (1968) intercom study, a participant heard another student apparently having a seizure. Those who believed they were the only listener were far more likely to help than those who believed four others could hear. This shows:
options: group polarisation
diffusion of responsibility
pluralistic ignorance
the self-serving bias
questions.explanation: Because participants could not see the others, they could not judge others' reactions, so the effect came from responsibility being spread across the group: each assumed someone else would help.

questions.stem: Which list gives Latane and Darley's steps that a bystander must pass through before helping, in order?
options: Interpret it as an emergency, act, notice the event, decide how to help, take responsibility
Notice the event, interpret it as an emergency, take responsibility, decide how to help, act
Take responsibility, notice the event, act, interpret it as an emergency, decide how to help
Decide how to help, act, notice the event, take responsibility, interpret it as an emergency
questions.explanation: A bystander must first notice the event, then interpret it as an emergency, then accept responsibility, then decide what to do, and finally act. A 'no' at any step means no help is given.

questions.stem: Weiner's attribution theory classifies explanations for success and failure along three dimensions. They are:
options: identity, comparison and categorisation
locus, stability and controllability
openness, stability and agreeableness
deviance, distress and dysfunction
questions.explanation: Weiner proposed that causes can be internal or external (locus), stable or unstable over time (stability), and controllable or uncontrollable (controllability). These attributions affect emotions and future motivation.

questions.stem: Max fails a test and says, 'I didn't study enough this time.' In Weiner's terms, this attribution is:
options: external, stable and uncontrollable
internal, stable and uncontrollable
external, unstable and uncontrollable
internal, unstable and controllable
questions.explanation: Lack of study is about Max (internal), can change next time (unstable) and is within his power (controllable). Weiner predicted this pattern supports persistence, whereas blaming low ability (internal, stable, uncontrollable) leads to giving up.

questions.stem: Weiner's theory predicts that a student who blames failure on a stable, uncontrollable cause, such as 'I'm just no good at maths', is most likely to:
options: expect to fail again and put in less effort in future
feel more motivated and study harder for the next test
attribute any later success to their own hard work
feel guilty, because they believe they could have tried harder
questions.explanation: If the cause seems permanent and out of one's control, there is little reason to try, so expectations and effort drop. Guilt is linked to controllable causes, such as not studying.

questions.stem: Rene Girard's scapegoat theory proposes that when tension and rivalry build within a community:
options: the group calmly negotiates until every member is equally satisfied
each member blames themselves, which reduces conflict over time
the group splits apart permanently into two equal-sized factions
the group unites by blaming and turning against a single victim
questions.explanation: Girard argued that rivalry spreads through imitation until a community resolves its crisis by uniting against a scapegoat, who is blamed for the trouble. Scapegoating more generally involves blaming an often powerless person or group for problems they did not cause.

questions.stem: During an economic downturn, some people blame a recently arrived migrant group for job losses that were caused by a recession. This illustrates:
options: latent learning
scapegoating
social facilitation
social loafing
questions.explanation: Scapegoating directs blame and hostility towards an out-group, often one with little power, for problems it did not cause. It can provide a simple explanation and a common enemy, strengthening the in-group.

questions.stem: Gordon Allport, in 'The Nature of Prejudice' (1954), argued that stereotypes arise partly because:
options: people naturally sort others into categories to simplify a complex world
people are born with fixed beliefs about every social group that they meet
stereotypes are always accurate summaries of group characteristics
only people with a mental disorder form generalisations about groups
questions.explanation: Allport saw categorisation as a normal cognitive process that saves effort, but warned it leads to overgeneralised beliefs that can harden into prejudice. Stereotypes are learnt, not inborn, and are often inaccurate.

questions.stem: Allport described a scale of prejudice that begins with antilocution (hostile talk) and moves through avoidance and discrimination. Why is this scale used in teaching about prejudice?
options: It shows that discrimination comes before prejudiced talk in every case
It shows how tolerated hostile talk can escalate towards more serious harm
It shows that hostile talk never leads to any harmful behaviour at all
It proves that prejudice always moves through every single stage within a week
questions.explanation: The scale suggests that accepting lower levels, such as jokes and hostile talk, can make more harmful behaviour seem acceptable. It describes a possible progression, not a fixed timetable that every case follows.

questions.stem: In Tajfel's minimal group studies, schoolboys were divided into groups on a trivial basis, such as a preference for one of two painters, and then shared out points. What did they tend to do?
options: Refuse to share any points until they knew who was in each group
Favour their own group, even giving up points to beat the other group
Share points equally, since the groups had no meaning to them at all
Favour the other group, to make a good impression on the researchers
questions.explanation: Even meaningless groups were enough to produce in-group favouritism, and boys often chose the option that maximised the difference between groups rather than their own group's total. This led to social identity theory.

questions.stem: What is the main conclusion drawn from the minimal group paradigm?
options: Simply being categorised into a group can be enough to produce in-group bias
In-group bias appears only when the groups compete for something of real value
In-group bias is caused by a history of conflict between two groups
People favour their own group only when they know its members well
questions.explanation: The groups had no history, no contact, no conflict and nothing real at stake, yet bias appeared, suggesting categorisation alone can trigger it. This contrasts with explanations that require competition for scarce resources.

questions.stem: John Turner's self-categorisation theory proposes that when a person's group identity becomes salient, they:
options: always obey the instructions of the person in charge, whatever the group
see themselves as an interchangeable member of the group and act in line with its prototype
focus only on their own unique personal traits and ignore whatever the group thinks
lose all sense of identity and act at random without any group norms at all
questions.explanation: Turner described depersonalisation: when a social identity is salient, people perceive themselves in terms of the group's prototype (its typical member) and adopt its norms. Personal identity becomes less important in that context.

questions.stem: Self-categorisation theory says which category feels most relevant depends on the context. Which example shows this?
options: A student always feels equally Australian in every single situation, whoever they are with
A student forgets their nationality whenever they are in a group of any size
A student's identity is fixed in early childhood and is not affected by context
An Australian student feels most 'Australian' when travelling in a group of overseas students
questions.explanation: Categories become salient when they best distinguish 'us' from 'them' in the situation; among overseas students, nationality stands out. In a classroom of Australians, a category such as year level or team might matter more.

questions.stem: In 1968 teacher Jane Elliott divided her Iowa primary class by eye colour and told them one group was superior. What did she observe?
options: Both groups ignored the labels completely and nothing changed in the classroom
The 'inferior' group did better on schoolwork because they tried harder to prove themselves
The students refused to accept the groups, so the exercise ended within minutes
The 'superior' group became bossy and the other group's schoolwork and confidence fell
questions.explanation: Within a day, children labelled superior became dominant and some were cruel, while those labelled inferior became withdrawn and did worse in class tasks. The exercise showed how quickly arbitrary labels can produce discrimination, but it raises ethical concerns about distress to children.

questions.stem: Norman Triplett (1898) noticed that cyclists rode faster when racing against others than when riding alone. This effect is called:
options: social facilitation
social loafing
group polarisation
deindividuation
questions.explanation: Social facilitation is improved performance in the presence of others. Triplett's work is often described as one of the first social psychology experiments.

questions.stem: Zajonc proposed that the presence of others increases arousal and strengthens a person's dominant response. Which prediction follows?
options: Everyone performs better with an audience, whatever their level of skill is
Everyone performs worse with an audience, whatever their skill level
An audience has no effect on performance, only on how people feel
An expert pianist plays better with an audience, but a beginner plays worse
questions.explanation: For well-learnt tasks the dominant response is correct, so arousal helps; for new or difficult tasks the dominant response is often an error, so performance drops. This explains why audiences sometimes help and sometimes hinder.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to reduce social loafing in group assignments. Which change is most likely to work?
options: Give one mark to the whole group, whatever each member did
Keep students anonymous so they feel less pressure to perform
Make each student's individual contribution identifiable and assessed
Make the groups larger so that more of the students share the work
questions.explanation: Social loafing is reduced when individual effort can be identified and evaluated, because people can no longer hide in the crowd. Larger groups and shared marks tend to increase loafing.

questions.stem: In Lewin, Lippitt and White's (1939) study of boys' clubs, groups with a democratic leader differed from those with an autocratic leader. Which was found?
options: All three leadership styles produced exactly the same behaviour in the boys
Democratic groups kept working when the leader left; autocratic groups tended to stop
Autocratic groups were the happiest and showed the least hostility of any group
Laissez-faire groups were the most productive and best organised of all the groups
questions.explanation: Autocratic groups were productive while the leader was present but showed more hostility or dependence, and work dropped when he left; democratic groups were more satisfied and kept working. Laissez-faire groups achieved the least.

questions.stem: A tight-knit cabinet, led by a strong leader, approves a risky plan. Members keep doubts to themselves and dissenting information is kept away from the group. Janis called this:
options: social facilitation
pluralistic ignorance
groupthink
group polarisation
questions.explanation: Groupthink occurs when the desire for agreement in a cohesive group overrides realistic evaluation, with symptoms such as self-censorship, an illusion of unanimity and members who shield the group from dissent. Janis used examples such as the Bay of Pigs invasion.

questions.stem: A jury whose members individually lean slightly towards a guilty verdict becomes strongly convinced of guilt after discussion. This illustrates:
options: the bystander effect
group polarisation
social loafing
the minimal group effect
questions.explanation: Group polarisation is the tendency for group discussion to strengthen members' initial leaning, making the group's position more extreme. It differs from groupthink, which centres on suppressing dissent to keep agreement.

questions.stem: Robert Sapolsky observed wild baboons in Kenya and measured their stress hormones. Which general finding did he report?
options: Social rank had no relationship with stress hormones in any baboon troop
Baboons had no stress hormones, so stress could not be measured in them
Lower-ranking baboons tended to have higher levels of stress hormones
Higher-ranking baboons always had the highest levels of stress hormones
questions.explanation: Sapolsky found that subordinate baboons generally had higher levels of glucocorticoids, linking low social status with chronic stress, although the pattern depends on the stability of the hierarchy. Such naturalistic observation is used to think about social status and health in humans.

questions.stem: Woods-Giscombe (2010) used focus groups with African American women to describe the 'Superwoman Schema', including an obligation to present an image of strength and to suppress emotions. Why is this research method suited to the aim?
options: Qualitative focus groups capture how participants themselves describe their experiences
Focus groups give precise numerical data that can be used to prove cause and effect
Focus groups remove the need for informed consent because people talk in groups
Qualitative data can be generalised to every population without further research
questions.explanation: The aim was to understand how women experience and explain strength and stress, which qualitative group discussion captures in participants' own words. Such research generates concepts that later quantitative studies can test, but it cannot by itself show cause and effect.

questions.stem: A review found that most participants in leading psychology journals come from Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic (WEIRD) societies. Why is this a problem for social psychology?
options: Research in other cultures is unethical, so it can never be carried out
Social behaviour is identical in every culture, so samples do not matter
Findings about groups may not apply to the many people who live in other cultures
WEIRD participants are always dishonest, so none of their answers can ever be trusted
questions.explanation: Behaviour in groups, such as conformity and in-group bias, varies across cultures, so findings from a narrow slice of humanity may not generalise. This Western-centric bias is an example of context shaping psychological knowledge.

questions.stem: Studies such as Milgram's obedience research and the Stanford Prison Experiment are often said to have changed psychology. In what way?
options: They showed that deception is always acceptable if the results are interesting
They proved that ethics committees slow research and should be abolished
They led researchers to stop studying social behaviour in groups entirely
They contributed to stricter ethical review, consent and protection from harm
questions.explanation: The distress caused to participants fed debates that led to stronger ethics review, informed consent, the right to withdraw and debriefing. Such studies could not be run today in their original form.
